stories.headline: Soccer's main characters: Man United, Como, PSG, Donnarumma
stories.summary: What are we watching this week? Man United are hoping for a rally, Como are magical to watch, PSG are the team to beat and we're worried about Gianluigi Donnarumma.
stories.body:
It's getting ridiculous in the best possible way. With each passing year, seemingly as teams realize that the extended Champions League league phase offers plenty of leeway if they lose a game or two, the guardrails slip a little bit more.

In 2024-25, teams averaged 1.63 goals per game in the league phase, a robust amount but not dramatically off of what we see in domestic leagues. In 2025-26, it was 1.69.

This year, through four matchdays, teams are averaging 2.02 goals per match. On Wednesday alone, six of nine matches saw at least five combined goals scored.

There were three 3-2 matches, including Fenerbahce's comeback win over Liverpool and lovely back-and-forth away wins for Manchester City (over RB Leipzig) and Real Madrid (over AEK Athens). And of course, there was Como's eye-popping 9-1 in over poor Lens; in their first Champions League campaign, the Italian side have scored 19 goals in their first four matches, winning three.

- UCL Talking Points: Are Como the real deal?

- Yamal makes more history for ruthless Barcelona

- Soccer's rich history of fan protests

The lack of consequence certainly has something to do with all this swashbuckling play, but maybe it's rubbed off on the rest of Europe? The season is still young, but scoring is up 7.8% in Ligue 1, 8.0% in the Bundesliga, 10.0% in LaLiga, and a whopping 20.1% in the Eredivisie and 23.9% in Serie A. Most of the increase has come from open-play, too -- it's not like teams are just earning a lot more penalties or something. (Meanwhile, Premier League scoring is actually down 2% so far this season. Fuddy duds.)

This is certainly a trend worth looking into, but for now I just want to say ... thank you. Goals are fun.

Let's once again look at five of soccer's main characters following another rousing Champions League matchday.

Main character No. 1: Manchester United's path forward

Ninety minutes is a long time. It's easy to forget that when you're an American fan accustomed to 3½-hour American football games, but on Tuesday at Old Trafford, 90 minutes was long enough for Manchester United to play maybe their most listless 45 minutes of the 2020s (a high bar to clear), watch their fans rain tennis balls onto the pitch in protest of administrative incompetence and a nine-match winless streak, grab a lifeline in the form of a penalty, miss said penalty, take advantage of a second chance via VAR, spend a good 20 minutes blowing a number of great chances to tie, and still have enough time left to tie, take the lead and hold on for what might (or might not) be a season-saving and trajectory-defining win.

Roma's two early goals made United look completely hapless, and when United fell behind 2-0, it almost looked as if Bruno Fernandes started trying to pick a fight and land a red card so he wouldn't have to watch the rest of the match. It even took Fernandes a second penalty attempt to get the home team on the board.

But from the moment his retake went into the net, Old Trafford seemed to flip into Fergie Time mode. Gone (for now) were the complaints and protests; back was the deep, guttural boom that stadium can generate when the home team scores a huge, late goal.

Roma have suffered some serious late-game issues in Champions League play, blowing a one-goal lead in a draw at Fenerbahce and now blowing a pair of two-goal leads in outright losses to United and Real Madrid. They've led in all four matches, but have just four points to show for it, and they certainly played a major role in their own demise Tuesday.

Still, something like this can definitely light a fire. Or at least, it had better.

While the entire Michael Carrick tenure looks a little different after Tuesday night's display, and the win kept their winless streak from reaching double digits, United's upcoming schedule is still pretty brutal: This Sunday, they host Aston Villa (who had a nice hot streak going before taking one on the chin against Barcelona on Tuesday), and when they return from the international break they visit Liverpool and Sporting CP, host Brentford and visit an equally desperate Newcastle. Without a major upgrade in form, the good feelings from this match won't last an incredibly long time.

During United's nine-match winless streak, the team suffered elements of poor fortune, scoring only six goals from shots worth 9.9 xG and allowing 18 from shots worth 16.6. But that isn't massive, and United had at least a slight negative xG differential in every game of this stretch. They were genuinely poor, and that obviously reflects on Carrick to some degree.

I actually liked the idea of making Carrick the full-time manager early on in his interim tenure last season, if only because he wasn't some overpaid Great Man type of manager -- the type that United typically try to hire -- and with Carrick in charge, the club might actually pursue a more sustainable roster-building strategy that isn't based entirely on the whims of said Great Man.

Carrick is simply a coach, and I thought that might work better. It certainly hasn't in 2026-27.

Still, it's not Carrick's fault that the club has spent so poorly in both the short and long term. It's not his fault that his left back options are either an injury-prone 31-year-old (Luke Shaw), a right back (Diogo Dalot) or a young center back (Ayden Heaven). It's not Carrick's fault that €75.9 million addition Carlos Baleba has managed only 397 minutes because of injuries (and just got hurt again), and it's not Carrick's fault that the club is, according to the estimates at FBref.com, paying Benjamin Sesko, Matthijs de Ligt, Harry Maguire, Mason Mount, Shaw, Noussair Mazraoui, Lisandro Martinez, Manuel Ugarte and Joshua Zirkzee nearly $100 million per year to not play close to the level required.

Carrick has gotten more out of players such as Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha, Kobbie Mainoo and even Fernandes than the last Great Man hire (Ruben Amorim) did. And while this is probably a lost season regardless -- United aren't winning the Champions League, and per the Opta projections they have only a 9.5% chance of finishing even in the Premier League top 7 -- it would benefit the club to not jump back into the Great Man waters just yet. But that will probably require Carrick generating quite a bit more magic in the coming weeks.

Main character No. 2: PSG and the biggest movers

Villarreal thumped Napoli and lost track meets against Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool to start Champions League play. They probably didn't expect to beat Paris Saint-Germain at home on Tuesday, but PSG were without star attackers Khvicha Kvaratshkelia and Ousmane Dembele, midfielder Marquinhos and also Nuno Mendes, maybe the best left back in the world.

Maybe they could keep things fun and competitive?

Nope. PSG led 4-0 after 17 minutes and rolled 6-0.

Even without that star power, they fielded a lineup loaded with Desire Doue, Maghnes Akliouche and Senny Mayulu up front, world-class midfielders Vitinha, Fabian Ruiz and Joao Neves and right back Achraf Hakimi, the best right back in the world. They brought World Cup-winning goal scorer Ferran Torres off the bench, and they got a goal from 17-year old fullback David Boly.

This is getting unfair. PSG at least made other teams think they had a chance the last couple of Champions League campaigns, easing into the league phase each year before shifting into gear when it counted. This time around, they've won their first four matches -- including matchups with Manchester City and Barcelona -- by a combined 20-5. Manager Luis Enrique is rotating as heavily as he ever has early in this season, both because of injury and because he wants to, and they've won 10 straight in all competitions by a combined 36-9. And the two-time defending Champions League winners' expected league phase point totals, per Opta's power ratings, have improved more than anyone else's in the competition.

Finally, those plucky Paris underdogs find some traction. Life's been so hard for them lately.

Three other teams have seen their expected point totals rise by at least 4.4 points: Real Madrid, who are also off to a perfect start -- albeit one full of late-game drama (and three one-goal wins) -- plus the ever-delightful Club Brugge and a Real Betis team that was off to a perfect start until Wednesday's 2-1 loss at Borussia Dortmund.

The biggest drops aren't quite as stark, primarily because they've all come from teams that weren't expected to do so hot anyway: Slavia Prague (down 4.2 points), Lille (3.9), AEK Athens (3.0) and Slovan Bratislava (2.6) have combined for one win and five points in 16 matches, though Slavia did frustrate Arsenal in a competitive 2-1 loss on Wednesday. It wouldn't be entirely surprising if one of these teams found their footing and made a run in the second half of league play, a la Bodo/Glimt last year.

OK, it would be a little surprising.

Others with higher expectations certainly haven't enjoyed the starts they were looking for: Porto (down 2.8) lost their first three before thumping Napoli on Wednesday, Roma (down 2.5) have suffered the aforementioned late-game collapses and have one win despite leading every match, and of course Manchester United (down 2.1) have had their well-publicized issues.

Main character No. 3: How the hell does a team score nine goals?

You can ask Manchester United: Como can play some pretty sexy ball sometimes. Even while balancing the rigors of domestic and continental play for the first time, they've lost just two of their first 14 matches in all competitions, and they've scored at least two goals 10 times and at least four goals four times. They've pummeled United and RB Leipzig and beaten Napoli away.

Cesc Fabregas seems to know what the heck he's doing as a manager, and his squad has enough fun attacking talent -- 22-year-old Nico Paz (six goals and eight assists in all competitions), 23-year-old Martin Baturina (five and two), veteran center forward Anastasios Douvikas (11 and one) -- that they've barely missed a more established player like Moise Kean, who's injured and has played only 158 minutes.

It's clear that this is a good team. But they scored nine goals Wednesday! On the road! Against a team from a Big Five league (albeit the fifth one)! How is that possible?

I guess the short answer is, "They couldn't miss." Como attempted 18 shots worth a massive 4.3 xG -- elite in its own right (and shameful on Lens' part) -- but overachieved that xG by 109%. Douvikas attempted three shots worth 1.7 xG and put all three in the net.

For the longer answer, however, I went to the film. They weren't just sending in lucky screamers from 30 meters - every shot they scored on was worth at least 0.12 xG, and all but one was from within 12 meters. This was a clinic in shotmaking, so I wanted to walk through each goal. You can follow along here:

- Goal No. 1, seventh minute: Douvikas from 3.0 meters (assist by Maximo Perrone). A short corner exchange sets up a cross to the far side, where Perrone heads it toward goal; he doesn't get much on it, but his shot becomes an assist for Douvikas, whom Lens tried to claim was offside.

- Goal No. 2, 32nd minute: Douvikas from 5.7 meters (assist by Alex Valle). On a quick transition, Paz gets the ball with space on the far right. He fires in a long and pretty off-target pass to Valle, but Valle saves it from going out of bounds and the flat-footed Lens defense doesn't notice Douvikas right in front of the goal for the tap-in.

- Goal No. 3, 40th minute: Paz from 10.0 meters (assist by Douvikas). A quick transition from Lucas da Cunha to Valle to Maxence Caqueret to Douvikas, and suddenly Paz has far too much space on the right. He fires into the top shelf, then pays tribute to fallen Spanish forward Jesus de Miguel.

- Goal No. 4, 47th minute: Lucas da Cunha from 12.1 meters (assist by Paz). After a good 30 seconds of possession, it's Paz to da Cunha to Yan Couto to da Cunha to Paz to a breaking da Cunha. Maybe the prettiest goal of the night, and Lens are officially broken.

- Goal No. 5, 53rd minute: Marc-Oliver Kempf from 8.1 meters (assist by Luis Milla). Caqueret quickly fizzes a ball to Luis Milla out on the left. He just as quickly fires a cross into the box, and Kempf heads it in.

- Goal No. 6, 57th minute: Douvikas from 15.6 meters (assist by Paz). After a series of horizontal passes near midfield, Como quickly go vertical and catch Lens flat-footed -- Perrone to Paz to Douvikas for an instant transition goal.

- Goal No. 7, 62nd minute: substitute Mattia Liberali from 10.8 meters (assist by Jacobo Ramon). More instant transition as Ramon simply frees Liberali on the right, and the 19-year-old races into the box and fires. Paz, Douvikas, Da Cunha and Milla have been subbed out, and Como continue to pour it on.

- Goal No. 8, 69th minute: substitute Martin Baturina from 11.9 meters (assist by Liberali). Shortly after Lens finally score, it's Baturina to Liberali, quickly back to a racing Baturina. Como played right through the middle on Lens, over and over.

- Goal No. 9, 90+1 minute: substitute Matteo Papaccioli from 11.7 meters (assist by Liberali). More fun interplay from the subs. After some quick passing, Liberali finds the 18-year-old Papaccioli in behind, and he converts. It's initially ruled offside, but it eventually counts.

My conclusion after all that is basically the same as how I started this section: Como play some sexy ball. Quick touches, lots of angles, lots of good chemistry. Lens had no idea where to look.

Watch this team whenever you can.

Main character No. 4: What's wrong with Donnarumma?

Gianluigi Donnarumma has been a celebrated shot-stopper since he forced his way into the AC Milan lineup 11 years ago at age 16. He hasn't ever been elite with his passing, but even possession-hungry clubs like PSG and Manchester City craved his services because of how well he keeps ball from going into net.

Over the past five seasons, he's been mostly excellent in this regard. Using Stats Perform's Goals Prevented measure -- which looks at the post-shot xG totals keepers face from shots on goal and compares that to the number of goals they allow -- he's been well on the positive range in all competitions.

See if you can spot a recent development.

Donnarumma's goals prevented, last 5 seasons

- 2021-22 (PSG): +5.0 (positive is good)

- 2022-23 (PSG): +7.8

- 2023-24 (PSG): +12.6

- 2024-25 (PSG): +2.0

- 2025-26 (Man City): +6.8

- 2026-27 (Man City): -1.2

He's had some stellar games this season: He had three big stops in a 1-0 win over Coventry City, for example (+1.8 goals prevented), plus three more in a 2-1 win over Bournemouth (+0.7) and six in a 3-0 win over Liverpool (+0.7). But he's in the middle of a pretty dire stretch: In his last six games in all competitions, starting with City's 4-2 loss to PSG, he's at minus-4.0 goals prevented. Simply breaking even might have turned losses to PSG and Aston Villa into draws, and he was relatively poor again on Wednesday against RB Leipzig, allowing two goals from shots on goal with a post-shot xG of 2.0.

City did hold on to beat RBL, but they've still lost three of their last seven matches in all competitions, and they've allowed 12 goals in those seven. I'm not going to pretend seven matches is a sign of his end as an elite goalkeeper, but it's been a costly stretch, and if not for City's offense, it would be even more costly.

Main character No. 5: The midway point best XI

Even if the league phase is entertaining but reasonably disposable content, I still enjoy taking a moment to celebrate awesome players from time to time, so since we're at the midway point of this phase, here's a quick Best XI for the competition to date.

Goalkeeper: David Raya, Arsenal. It's hard to evaluate Raya because he doesn't typically have much to do behind Arsenal's defense, but he's saved 10 of 14 shots on target for a solid +1.8 goals prevented, and he has decent involvement in the buildup game. He had to make four saves against a game Slavia squad on Wednesday, but did so. Backup: Yann Sommer, Club Brugge

Right back: Achraf Hakimi, PSG. I could tell you his stats -- one assist, 12 chances created, 57 line-breaking passes received (most of any defender) -- but "best right back in the world" should do. Backup: Givairo Read, Feyenoord

Center back: Mykola Matvilenko, Shakhtar Donetsk. He's completed 57 progressive carries (second among defenders) and 36 progressive passes (fifth), and he has 1,401 meters of carry distance (first). The 30-year-old is a stabilizing force and strong buildup guy for a team currently in position to advance. Backup: Pau Cubarsi, Barcelona

Center back: Dayot Upamecano, Bayern Munich. Upamecano's another hard-to-evaluate player because he's put on such islands in Bayern's high-line system that you can probably remember him in the middle of a lot of breakdowns. But he's in those awkward spots because he's such a trustworthy 1v1 defender, and he's a high-level passer too. Backup: Brandon Mechele, Club Brugge

Left back: David Raum, RB Leipzig. Among defenders, Raum is third in chances created (10), eighth in progressive passes (34), second in crosses (34) and second in tackle attempts (21). He's been busy for RBL's strained defense, but he's always a pretty important contributor in attack too. Backup: Joao Cancelo, Barcelona

Defensive midfield: Declan Rice, Arsenal. Most progressive carries of any midfielder (48), most progressive passes (63), most carry distance (1,487 meters), third-most line-breaking passes (54), even eighth-most ball recoveries (24). He's brilliant and indefatigable. Backup: Elliot Anderson, Manchester City

Central midfield: Fabian Ruiz, PSG. He has four goals (most of any midfielder), 14 shots (most), 283 passes received (most), 58 progressive passes (second-most) and 57 line-breaking passes (second-most). He seems to be getting better at 30. Backup: Vitinha, PSG

Attacking midfield: Nico Paz, Como. Maybe the player of the competition so far. He's scored three goals with five assists, he's received 60 line-breaking passes (only Lamine Yamal has more), and I mean, just watch him. He seems to make everyone around him more creative than they otherwise would be. (And he's only 22.) Backup: Jude Bellingham, Real Madrid

Right win: Lamine Yamal, Barcelona. Another no-brainer. He also has seven combined goals (three) and assists (four), and he's received the most line-breaking passes (73), attempted the most ground duels (70) and won the most 1v1s in the box (five). He's even made the most ball recoveries in the attacking third (nine), including an easy one for a goal on Tuesday.

He's the best winger in the world, and he's still just 19. Unfair. Backup: Bradley Barcola, Liverpool

Center forward: Harry Kane, Bayern Munich. I wanted to get a little creative and give this spot to someone other than the reigning Ballon d'Or winner, but Kane is tied for second in combined goals (four) and assists (three), he's attempted the most shots (20), and even with slightly below-standard finishing -- four goals from 4.1 xG -- he's just the most complete player up front right now. Backup: Tasos Douvikas, Como

Left wing: Desire Doue, PSG. He's seventh in the competition in combined goals (three) and assists (two), and he's only played 218 of 360 minutes. Explosive, creative, ridiculously confident and, yes, still only 21. Backup: Zlatko Tripic, Viking

stories.headline: Best of MLB playoffs: Moments, games that defined October
stories.summary: A week after the Brewers completed their title run, here's what we won't soon forget from the 2026 postseason.
stories.body:
Whether you love dramatic finishes, thrilling moments or incredible individual performances, the 2026 MLB playoffs provided a little bit of everything.

A week after the Milwaukee Brewers lifted their first World Series championship trophy, we asked our MLB experts to pick the best single moments, games and series from the entire postseason -- along with their lasting October impressions.

From wild-card thrillers to World Series heroics, here is the best of the best from every round of the 2026 postseason.

What was the defining moment of the entire MLB playoffs?

Bradford Doolittle: As it turned out, I was at all the Brewers' playoff games except the two in San Diego. So I was there when Ty France launched a ball off the American Family Field ceiling, or some wires or whatever, and Jackson Chourio stuck with the play and caught it and the Brewers won. All through the rest of the postseason, Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy alluded to the play as Bob Uecker reaching down from the great beyond to swat that ball down to help the Brewers.

I can't get on board with that, but at the same time it was a moment when I felt like Milwaukee was destined to win. And all through the Brewers' run, it felt like so many borderline moments, whether resolved by luck or skill, went Milwaukee's way. You take baseball's best team and then give it the majority of the breaks and you have what we ended up with: a champion that went 11-2 en route to winning it all.

David Schoenfield: Given the strength of the top teams in the NL compared to the obvious weaknesses of the best AL teams, it felt like the NLCS between the Brewers and Dodgers was going to decide the eventual World Series champ. After losing Game 1 with Tarik Skubal, the Dodgers at least knew they had 2025 postseason hero Yoshinobu Yamamoto going in Game 2. Then came the bottom of the third inning and Jake Bauers' walk.

How can a walk be the defining moment of the MLB playoffs? Because it was a 12-pitch walk with Bauers grinding and battling and fouling off six pitches with a 3-2 count before finally drawing ball four. It wiped out Yamamoto. Christian Yelich followed with a go-ahead two-run single and Yamamoto was out of the game, unable to finish the inning. The Dodgers would actually retake the lead, but with Yamamoto gone early, the Brewers went back ahead against the Dodgers' second-line relievers. The Brewers had won games that Skubal and Yamamoto started. Neither would throw another pitch.

Jeff Passan: If anything encapsulated the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers, it was the fifth inning of Game 3 of the World Series. After Christian Yelich's excellent baserunning instincts saved the inning from ending on a force play at second, the Brewers rapped two-out hit after two-out hit en route to scoring eight runs and extending a 2-0 advantage to 10-0. This wasn't a moment, per se; it was 26 minutes of horror for Tampa Bay. And those minutes birthed a moment that's undeniable: the one in which the Rays understood just how different the Brewers really were.

What was the single best game of the entire MLB postseason?

Buster Olney: The Padres could've upended the Brewers' championship run in the division series between the two teams, and it looked like they might be in position to do that in Game 2, when they handed a 3-2 lead to the most feared closer in the game, Mason Miller.

The right-hander, asked to get the last six outs, zipped through three Milwaukee hitters in the eighth, needing only 12 pitches. But in the ninth, the Brewers' hitters did what they became known for in October: grinding through at-bats. With Miller suddenly struggling to command his fastball, Christian Yelich worked a walk, and after Yelich stole second, Sal Frelick walked. Then Miller's slider began to flatten out as his pitch count mounted, and pinch hitter Gary Sanchez stared him down for another walk, loading the bases.

Miller's pitch count had climbed over 30, and with his slider failing him, he leaned into his fastball against Jackson Chourio - and the 22-year-old swung confidently, aggressively. Miller's 40th pitch was a 101 mph fastball, and Chourio lashed a single to center to drive in the winning run. From that point forward, no one seriously threatened the Brewers.

Alden Gonzalez: This might not have been the best game of the postseason, per se, but it's one that shouldn't be lost to history. The Braves decided to push their ace, Chris Sale, back to Game 3 of the NLDS, a risky decision that felt calamitous after the Dodgers took Game 1.

Atlanta's hopes of maintaining a reasonable chance of winning the series would fall on the shoulders of its bullpen. And then Ray Kerr, a minor league journeyman who famously once worked at 7-Eleven, and Didier Fuentes, a 20-year-old who graduated to the big leagues much earlier than expected, combined for 19 of the Braves' 27 outs in an improbable victory, delivering 6⅓ innings of one-run ball.

The Braves went on to lose the next two games and were thus eliminated, but Game 2 of the NLDS was a reminder of what makes postseason baseball so great -- the surprises that define October, the guys you've never heard of who become heroes.

Jorge Castillo: The Brewers won the World Series in five games, but the matchup was plenty closer than that indicates. Three of the five games were decided by one run, including my pick for the best game of the postseason: Game 4 at Tropicana Field.

Tampa Bay appeared on its way to getting swept when Cooper Pratt homered off Ian Seymour in the 12th inning to give the Brewers a 3-2 lead and move them within three outs of the first championship in franchise history. But the Rays, after not scoring since the fourth inning, scored two runs on an error and four straight singles without recording an out to keep their season alive.

The teams combined to use 15 pitchers. The Rays emptied their bench. Ben Williamson, the final player off that bench, delivered the walk-off single -- a ball that bounced off the artificial turf in front of home plate and into shallow right field. For one night, the Rays had hope.

What was the best series of the playoffs, from any round?

Jesse Rogers: If you can believe it, there were only two series that went the distance this October: The Braves beating the Phillies in the wild-card round and the Guardians outlasting the White Sox in their division series matchup.

The latter turned out to be one of the best of October as it featured a little bit of everything: Road teams winning the first four games, come-from-behind victories and dramatic moments -- like when Cleveland lefty Erik Sabrowski struck out Munetaka Murakami with the bases loaded in Game 5. Both fan bases were energized throughout the series, providing more energy in the building than some other contests in October. Oh, and Cleveland stormed back from 2-0 in the series to win it. It was a good one.

Olney: The Padres were the hottest team in the majors the last two months of the regular season, and in the divisional round, they faced the best team from 2026, the Brewers. It felt to a lot of folks in the game that the eventual champion would emerge from this series, and after some great moments -- Chourio's game-winning hit off Miller in Game 2, Garrett Mitchell intercepting a would-be home run in Petco Park -- Milwaukee survived the Padres and went 8-1 in its remaining postseason games.

Gonzalez: Buster is correct. There was no better series than Brewers-Padres. It lasted only four games, but every one of them contained a defining moment (don't forget Game 3, when Michael King, pitching two days after his start, took down the last two innings to save the Padres' season on a night when both Adrian Morejon and Mason Miller were unavailable).

The Brewers went on to sweep the Dodgers in the NLCS and breeze past the Rays in the final round. By the end, it was clear that the Padres were their biggest challenge. If any one moment goes the other way -- France's fly ball, Chourio's at-bat, King's appearance, Machado's fly ball -- we might be looking at a different World Series champion right now.

What is your lasting takeaway of this MLB postseason?

Passan: The return of small-market, low-payroll teams to the apex of the sport amid a labor negotiation in which the owners continue to suggest small-market, low-payroll teams can't compete in the current environment. The league's point about the recent history of World Series participants coming from larger markets and payrolls is fair, but multiple owners, speaking on the condition of anonymity, acknowledged that the Brewers and Rays facing off in the World Series did little to help reinforce their argument that a salary cap's main purpose would serve competitive balance.

Schoenfield: The perception -- incorrect -- that the Brewers were some scrappy, small-ball team that punched above its weight and slapped the ball around to victory. Nonsense. Yes, the Brewers have made some wonderful moves through the years to obtain players other teams didn't want, especially flipping Josh Hader for Robert Gasser (their Game 3 starter) and Esteury Ruiz, who was later traded for William Contreras. They got closer Trevor Megill for nothing, and Jake Bauers emerged off the scrap heap to have a star turn in 2026.

But this team has talented players up and down the roster: Brice Turang was a first-round pick in 2018, Garrett Mitchell in 2020, Sal Frelick in 2021. Yelich, Andrew Vaughn and DL Hall were first-round picks by other organizations. Cooper Pratt was a sixth-round pick, but regarded as a first-round talent and signed for second-round money. Jacob Misiorowski was a second-round pick. Jackson Chourio was the No. 2 prospect in the game. Luis Lara is a 21-year-old speedster who can run everything down in the outfield.

Yes, the Brewers have a different style -- they had the highest ground ball rate in the majors -- but they still hit the ball hard. They had the seventh-highest average exit velocity in the regular season and the third-most balls hit at 100-plus mph. They draw walks -- second-most in the regular season and 15 more than their opponents during the postseason. Most of the position players can run as well. They draft athletes and develop them and get their pitchers to throw harder or throw more strikes.

They actually struck out a few more times than their opponents during the playoffs. Sure, they hit "only" 13 home runs in 14 playoff games -- but they outhomered their opponents 13-4. They won with scouting, player development, execution, plate discipline and enough home run power. They have good baseball players. That's why they won.

Doolittle: As soon as the World Series matchup was set, I was fixated on the television ratings. I wasn't so much concerned with comparisons to the past two years, which both featured ideal conditions to produce big ratings. I was really curious how they would compare to 2023 -- the Rangers-Diamondbacks matchup that did not fare well in the ratings game. It was a short series, like this one, and also didn't feature markets favored by television, or at least as I understand the subject.

This series by all accounts fared way better than that one, with around 11.7 million viewers on average as compared to around 9.1 million in 2023. Here is my contention: People were thrilled by this matchup and this was true because of how these teams play baseball and, most crucially, because they were the respective top seeds in their leagues. It was the same matchup we would have gotten if we were still using the format in place from 1903 to 1968. In 2023, by contrast, we were watching a 5-seed against a 6-seed.

I think this matters -- a lot -- and I think favoring a format that rewards regular season excellence should be paramount when we consider such things going forward.

stories.headline: Every AFL club's 2026 draft plans, prospects linked, and live trade options
stories.summary: ESPN's AFL Draft expert Jasper Chellappah looks at every club's plans, its prospects linked, and potential live trade options.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL Draft is two weeks away, and there's a clearer picture on what each club's draft plans are.

You can expect around 65 selections to be made in what has become a deep draft. The mix from 15 to 30 is incredibly even, and the prospects deserving of an opportunity at AFL level runs well past the 65 picks that we'll see across the nights of November 19 and 20.

Amongst the club intel and prospects being targeted at each pick are potential trades to watch for on draft night. Port Adelaide, Carlton and Brisbane will be beholden to where bids land for their star academy prospects, and the selections they hold could be on the move in live draft night trades. Collingwood, Essendon and Adelaide are amongst the clubs mooted to be interested in trading up the order to secure their targets.

It's worth noting that the arrival of Tasmania has repercussions on this year's draft; clubs are more keen to get in now to secure young talent, but it also means draft capital is worth less in future years. Trading up the draft order will be as hard as it's ever been in the live trade era, meaning we could see a host of potential trades never come to fruition.

Included in the details on the Bombers, Tigers and Eagles are the start of second round compensation picks they will receive at the beginning of night two. These come about after a club-tied prospect -- which will be Port Adelaide's Dougie Cochrane -- is taken with a pick prior to their top five selections.

As we approach November's AFL Draft, these are the draft plans, prospects linked, and live trade options for all 18 clubs.

Adelaide
Draft picks: 15, 32, 35, 43, 56, 92, 110

List needs: Midfield quality, outside speed

Adelaide had a quiet trade period and knocked back a swathe of picks for Nick Murray, meaning Hamish Ogilvie's team holds its natural first-rounder plus two seconds to top up a list hunting a premiership. They're valuable selections, but without any manoeuvring they've left themselves behind two Port Adelaide picks in the second round, amongst a nest of talented SA products. Without making a move on draft night the Power will have first dibs on the local crop.

The Crows had a late NGA application for rebounding defender Jake Eime rejected after being alerted to his Indigenous heritage through the SANFL too late in the piece. That shouldn't dissuade them from using a first-rounder on the local product. Eime has the speed and dare to become an offensive weapon off halfback and improve the quality of ball going inside 50.

They'll likely have one of the top three key defenders in the class available, but it won't be Mitch Harris who is firming as a top 10 selection. Clancy Snell would add to their key defensive depth as a high-upside interceptor out of Gippsland, but it would be a touch early for SA captain Kodah Edwards despite his unique mix of forward impact and contested gruntwork.

The best midfielder available at 15 could be Toby Krasna. The Vic Metro on-baller runs both ways and offers some flair with ball in hand on the outside of contests. The versatility and ready-made body of Lochie Burrows would appeal with a view to eventually playing through the midfield. Potential sliders include athletic third tall Wil Malady and tough WA midfielder Leo Steed; the latter should be right in the frame as a piece to immediately push for senior selection.

Late in the second round the lethal left foot of Wil Antrobus should appeal and Gus Kennedy's toughness as a defender with midfield flashes suits. With Adelaide in need of best 23 contenders through the midfield, local products Archie Van Dyk and Memphis Webb will warrant consideration as mature bodies late in the draft. NGA Anthony Long is a backend draft proposition but has serious tricks in the forward half and is deserving of a main list spot.

Brisbane
Draft picks: 21, 27, 28, 45, 79, 97, 115

List needs: Key defender depth

The Lions have another academy gun on their hands, and Caylen Murray has risen to the precipice of the top 10 this season. Granting Keidean Coleman's trade wish effectively ensured Brisbane would have the collateral to match a bid, but they'll have contingencies in place depending on where it lands.

It could come as early as Queensland rivals Gold Coast at pick 8, which would require 1732 points including a 20% loading on grand finalists. Their first two picks only make up 1254 points right now so the Lions will have moves up and down the board with their three second-rounders depending on where the bid lands.

In Murray they're getting a natural Dayne Zorko replacement with excellent ball skills out of defence. His composure under pressure is a highlight and there are midfield traits to be uncovered at the next level.

If the Lions are able to hold onto a second-rounder Jake Soutar presents as the most ready-made defender in the pool. The 20-year-old took out East Perth's fairest and best this season and plays with fantastic aggression in the air, intercepting and kickstarting transition. Darcy Szerszyn is a similar type in the top 30 mix with good athletic traits but underwent an injury-interrupted year.

Benji Van Rooyen is a long-term ruck prospect to look at towards the end of the draft and at 197cm Tate Hodgson has the defensive aptitude to develop into a reliable key defender.

Carlton
Draft picks: 13, 18, 31, 50, 61, 72, 90, 108

List needs: Classy ball users, long-term ruck

Blues fans have been looking forward to this draft for years. Father-son Cody Walker is a bona fide top pick with elite traits through the midfield and he will land at Princes Park no matter where taken, but it's unlikely to be in the first two selections on draft night.

That's a good result for the Blues with live trades in the works depending on where a bid comes. If it lands at pick 3 they'll require 2178 points and their first two selections will equate to 2019 points after an earlier bid on Cochrane. Carlton can do that with a small deficit on their 2027 first-rounder. If Richmond doesn't bid on Walker and he falls to 4 or 5 there will be clubs keen on those selections, and Carlton can capitalise. A slide back to Essendon's 17 from 13 would allow them to match and move their second-rounder up from 31 to 25.

Getting back into the draft early in the second round will give the Blues access to a group of good ball users including Jackson Phillips and Harvie Cooke. Phillips is the running wingman while Cooke is a high-IQ midfielder with talent to play ahead of the ball. George Dimer and Marlon Neocleous are exciting small forwards to consider and Ethan Herbert is the project ruck around this range.

Later in the piece WA's Benji Van Rooyen could appeal as an apprentice to Marc Pittonet and mature-ager Brady Wright would add immediate competition for spots up forward.

Collingwood
Draft picks: 11, 30, 67, 68, 70, 88, 106

List needs: Midfield speed, key position depth

The Pies own a pick in an exciting spot of the draft. There are a cluster of different prospects deserving of top 10 consideration that will be available, but one that may be gone at that point is Sam Gayfer. The nephew of 1990 premiership defender Mick has steadily risen this year as a pack-splitting key forward and the Pies have been one of his biggest fans. Justin Leppitsch would need to part with at least a future first-rounder to a club like Port Adelaide or Gold Coast to ensure they can get him.

If they stay put, Tyson Bradley appeals as the full back of the future and could play senior football early. He's a strong one-on-one defender and reliable distributor with the character to be a future leader of the club. Clancy Snell put in a good performance for Collingwood's VFL side but is an interceptor that may take more time to develop.

Leo Steed is the pick of the midfielders in this bracket, with the WA on-baller offering a mix of defensive application and contested ball-winning that fits alongside Nick Daicos. High-flying forward Wil Malady will be taken around this mark as well.

In the second round the Pies could look to Harvie Cooke and George Gale as midfield options, and mature-age forward options later in the piece include Brady Wright and Jack Slattery who could add immediate depth behind Jesse Hogan and Dan McStay.

Essendon
Draft picks: 1, 17, 25, 80, 98 (plus second round compensation pick)

List needs: Best available talent

The Bombers are at the bottom of their rebuild and hold the first overall selection a decade after taking Andy McGrath at no. 1. Similarly to 2016 and as opposed to recent drafts, there's no consensus top prospect in the open pool.

Expect a bid on Dougie Cochrane at one which Port Adelaide will quickly match, then the draft really begins. Ethan Drever is the slight favourite at no. 2 after a blistering campaign for club and state. The explosive midfielder stayed injury free and produced gaudy numbers enroute to Vic Country's MVP and GWV Rebels's best and fairest. His elite transition game alongside Dyson Sharp and Sullivan Robey will surely appeal.

Arki Butler is a rare archetype to come through the elite pathways and presents as the forward match-winner of the crop. His name has been firmly in contention for the top spot all season and the need to add talent alongside Nate Caddy in the forward 50 is real. Ruck Harry Van Hattum and classy ball user Heath Mellody deserve consideration here as well, but Drever and Butler have the inside lane two weeks out from the draft.

The Dons will have a look at moving up from 17 with additional picks - that could work for either of Port Adelaide or Carlton live on draft night as they look to maximise their draft hands while still matching bids. The key defensive option in the teens is Tyson Bradley, a no-nonsense negator with leadership plaudits. Toby Krasna is in this range as a talented outside midfielder with flair, while George Dimer is in demand as a speedy small forward with tricks.

In the 20s Essendon should be looking at upside swings. Jack Pickett was the leading key forward prospect coming into the year but a season on the sidelines due to an ACL rupture could make him a bargain on night two. Similarly, Koby LeCras adds size and polish out of WA and Lachie Hicks could prove the midfield steal with his blend of speed and endurance as a former track athlete.

The Dons have some interest in Jake Soutar as a mature-age interceptor to replace Jordan Ridley, but will also need to account for a bid on Blake Justice that likely lands towards the back end of the second round. The NGA graduate has a unique mix of speed and size that could even see him attract a bid early on night two.

Fremantle
Draft picks: 19, 40, 60, 63, 78, 96, 114

List needs: Lockdown defender, high-upside talent

Dockers fans don't need reminding how close they've come to that elusive first premiership, but they've continued to build through the draft and keep their premium picks during contention.

At the end of the first round Jake Eime warrants consideration as a halfback dasher alongside Jordan Clark. He takes the game on with speed and can use the ball well while still defending. Jake Soutar has been closely linked as the mature-age option to add to their best 23, but sits between Freo's first two picks on many boards. They would need to trade up or take him with 19.

With 40 being pushed out on the second night they could look towards local talent in Harvey Spawton-Guy whose competitiveness as a key forward stands out. Tom Brown has been overlooked by some but offers reliability in defence and it would be a brilliant result if hard-running midfielder George Gale was still on the board. The goalkicking prowess of Archie Elliott should also appeal in this range of the draft.

The Dockers will be keen to get Finlay Yeo into the club as buzz continues to grow on the NGA talent. He's gifted below his knees and makes things happen through the midfield and up forward. Cam Maynard has offered mercurial moments as a small forward and finished second in the 20m sprint at the combine, but Lucas Robinson has fallen away this season and will be a rookie consideration for Fremantle.

Geelong
Draft picks: 36, 57, 62, 75, 93, 111

List needs: Defensive depth, high-upside projects

The Cats did their work in the trade period by getting Rowan Marshall and Jordan Ridley into the club. Making those moves is made easier knowing Stephen Wells does his best work late in the draft.

Lachie Hicks presents as the high-upside swing in the second round, similarly to Max Holmes in 2020. Hicks has elite athletic pedigree state records through his juniors in track but also put together an impressive campaign as a midfielder. His ball use is preventing him from being a first round option but there's a lot to work with in a good development program.

Billy Wigmore is an excellent interceptor with a build similar to that of Tom Stewart but his draft range begins earlier than pick 36. Sam Dever has been linked as an athletic utility that looks most at home off halfback at 189cm, while the best local product is Noah Williams who played through frustrating injuries all season. He's a smaller inside midfielder with good defensive instincts that could cut his teeth as a lockdown defender.

Gold Coast
Draft picks: 8, 81, 85, 103

List needs: Key position depth

The Suns have Sam Collins turning 33 next year and lost Ben King to free agency. It leaves them exposed at either end over the next few years and they have real need to address their tall stocks with their first open pool top 10 selection since Bailey Humphrey in 2022.

The best key forward in the draft is Sam Gayfer, a brave aerialist possessing the best vertical jump in combine history. His ability to bring the ball to ground with his pack-crashing attitude should appeal to Damien Hardwick. At the other end Mitch Harris and Clancy Snell offer different styles of key defenders. Harris can lockdown on the best key forwards and intercept in his own right, while Snell is the ultra-aggressive interceptor of the pool. Being a country Victorian will help the Suns when assessing their ability to retain talent.

This is the start of Wil Malady's range in the draft, and there's a chance of a slider like Gus Teixeira or Heath Mellody that could make Gold Coast's choice easy.

Local academy product Archie Hill should find his way onto the list as a running defender that plays with energy and dare.

GWS
Draft picks: 9, 20, 26, 59, 77, 86, 104

List needs: Midfield talent, key position depth

It's all about Ethan Matthews on night one, the best Giants Academy prospect to come through the ranks since Tom Green. Matthews is a classy midfielder that racks it up with clean hands and quick decision making off his preferred left foot, and will deservedly be a top 10 pick.

The Giants are in an awkward spot at pick 9, expecting a bid to land before that selection and potentially coming from crosstown rivals the Swans at pick 6. It makes matching the bid easy but look for them to maximise their draft hand by trading on the clock.

In the middle of the second round they will have a few names on the board. George Dimer should be right up there as a high-character small forward with tricks around goal and a willingness to move interstate. Athletic utility Sam Devers could play anywhere across the ground after a strong finish to an injury-plagued year, while the fascinating call will be on Mason McGroder. The Swans Academy defender has foregone a promising international long jump career to pursue football and although raw boasts elite athletic traits in defence. The Giants could make the Swans sweat with a bid in the 20s for the high-upside athlete.

Hawthorn
Draft picks: 29, 37, 71, 94, 107, 112

List needs: Outside run, halfback depth

The Hawks are beautifully set with depth challenging at just about every position. Bringing in Ben King and Zach Merrett made them the biggest winners of the trade period and they still held onto two valuable selections in a deep draft.

A bid on NGA product Keenan Boi is a chance to arrive before their first pick. The half forward plays through contact with strength and makes good decisions under pressure. He's been likened to Sam Powell-Pepper in his attack on the ball and man in the forward half.

In that second round Harrison Chapman offers a unique blend of strong running at 190cm. He looks most at home on a wing where he can use the ball well in space. Albert MacGowan also has the runs on the board to warrant a second round selection as a high-marking wingman. Wil Antrobus is another who can provide transition run, and comes with the added bonus of an elite left foot out of defence that suits the Hawks's style of play.

Hawthorn will be waiting to see if a bid comes for Cooper Hodge. The son of champion Luke looks most at home in defence but has also had promising outings through the midfield in a potential sign of things to come. If a bid doesn't come in the national draft the Hawks will likely take him with their last pick.

Melbourne
Draft picks: 4, 14, 48, 52

List needs: Key defensive talent, ball-winning midfielders

It's been a perpetual cycle of trading into and up draft boards that has reaped rewards for the Dees, who are building their next generation on the fly. They snagged a top 10 pick from the Suns in the Christian Petracca deal last year and made an early move with Port Adelaide to get even higher up the board.

Now, they're in a fantastic position to snap up one of their top four targets. Names in the mix will include Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody. There's every chance those are the first names off the board in the open pool, and you can expect this to be the final place where a bid on Cody Walker would come.

If those three are gone, there will be a fun mix at the top of their board. Similarly to Luke Jackson in 2019, the Dees could opt to give a ruckman the ultimate apprenticeship under the best to do it in the modern era. Harry Van Hattum is deserving of a pick this high - he blends elite athleticism, skill with ball in hand and physicality at a genuine ruck size. The 205cm enforcer plays with aggression in the mould of Brodie Grundy and, similarly to Grundy, may not have the forward craft to play alongside Gawn early on.

Gus Teixeira is the forward-half midfielder with power and scoreboard impact. He can play through centre bounces but will start his career at half forward where he finds a lot of the ball and doesn't need much space to impact.

The wildcard here is Mitch Harris. The premier defender of the pool is equally adept at locking down and intercepting, playing with an air of calm and composure. His range starts here and the SA product is very much in play for the Demons as a ready-made foil for Jake Lever and Dan Turner with senior football under his belt.

At pick 14 Leo Steed should be right in the mix as an in-and-under midfielder that can run hard both ways on the outside. He plays at a high cadence and has a strong body of work in the WAFL. Toby Krasna and Lochie Burrows are other midfield types that deserve consideration, while the other first-round key defenders in Clancy Snell and Tyson Bradley will be options if they opt against Harris earlier.

Brady Wright or Jack Slattery offer immediate forward depth late in the draft and Marcus Prasad is a small forward with clean hands that the Dees could opt for despite not having rights on through their NGA. Benji Van Rooyen could play alongside his brother as he learns the ropes under Gawn.

North Melbourne
Draft picks: 33, 49, 66, 74, 84, 102

List needs: Key position talent, classy ball users

North put their chips in for Nick Blakey and as a result will be without a top-20 pick for the first time since 2019. It signals a new era for the Shinboners as they mount a charge up the ladder under coach Jaymie Graham.

The Roos enter at pick 33, which will extend out a few spots after bids and compensation picks at the top of night two. Billy Wigmore is the type of defender they've been desperate for - the interceptor can play above his size but also roll off smaller forwards to chop out in the air and assist his key defenders. The third tall could play senior football early to add to North's best 23 depth.

Despite a clear need for key position talent, they've taken Matt Whitlock and Blake Thredgold with premium picks and could instead opt for good ball users around the park with an aim to move the ball with more speed. That puts classy halfback Wil Antrobus in the mix as a weapon to utilise out of defence. Further afield lies the upside of rangy outside midfielder Harrison Chapman who has exciting upside as a transition runner, and this is the range busy small forward Marlon Neocleous is expected to be taken. Albert MacGowan and Sam Devers are other running types that could play senior football next year after strong finishes to the year.

Key forward Aidan McCartney has nominated the Roos as a father-son after being in the Swans Academy and has exciting traits despite being sidelined this year with a hip injury.

Port Adelaide
Draft picks: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46, 65, 101

List needs: Midfield depth, key position talent

Night one is all about Dougie Cochrane, the near-consensus top prospect amongst clubs in 2026. Through the Zak Butters free agency compensation and smart manoeuvring in the trade period the Power are well-prepared to match a bid on the academy star at pick one, and have set themselves up with three first-rounders next year with an eye to Zemes Pilot and Louis Salopek.

Selections 7 and 12 remain on the table, but it will take a significant offer for Port to cop a deficit on their 2027 first-rounder. If they moved 7 down in a trade with St Kilda or Collingwood they would then be dealing with a significant deficit on their 2027 selection, so a trade of pick 12 looks more likely. Adelaide and Essendon can trade up from 15 and 17 respectively without impacting Port's ability to match a bid on Cochrane, which could land the Power a future selection or an extra second-rounder this year.

The second round will have a fun mix of local talent. Halfback dasher Jake Eime would be a priority if he was to slide and SA captain Kodah Edwards is right in the frame. His hands in the contest and scoreboard impact up forward offers unique versatility. Ethan Herbert would be a long-term pick with a view to his upside as a ruckman with fantastic contested numbers, and Gabe Patterson presents as a powerful small forward that can break games open. Ball-winners Archie Van Dyk and Memphis Webb are later propositions that could come on quicker than expected in the right environment.

Outside of SA, Jack Watkins has steadily risen this year and would be a smart choice later in the piece as a goalkicking half forward, while Cody Templeton and Marcus Prasad are other smalls in a similar draft range. WA's George Gale is a big-bodied midfielder with excellent endurance in the Willem Drew mould and ball magnet Jordan Knapp has the midfield chops to make it at the next level despite his slender frame. Both will be right in the mix as Port looks to the next generation of on-ballers. Xavier Ladbrook looms as the best key defensive option outside of the first night but will take time to add the size required to play at AFL level.

Richmond
Draft picks: 2, 5, 44, 99 (plus second round compensation pick)

List needs: Best available talent

The Tigers made a big trade to land a second top five pick and maximise their talent before Tasmania enters the competition. It gives them an enviable hand but they'll need to be smart in how they play it with West Coast and Melbourne picking between their selections.

They've been closely linked to Harry Van Hattum. If they have HVH at the top of the board they'll need to use pick 2 on him, with his aggression making him a natural successor to skipper Toby Nankervis. There's every chance they have another name or two ahead of Van Hattum, however, which means intel on Melbourne will be vital here. There's no guarantee he will be available at 5, but that's the limits of his draft range with Richmond to pounce if still on the board.

All of Ethan Drever, Arki Butler and Heath Mellody will be considered at pick 2. Drever is the explosive midfielder that fits comfortably alongside Sam Lalor and Taj Hotton as the midfield of the future. Arki Butler is the much-needed firepower up forward to pair with their project talls, and Mellody provides the class and running power off halfback and through the midfield that has been lacking under Adem Yze.

If Drever is taken by Essendon, Butler will be the live favourite to land at Tigerland. He has been at the pointy end of the draft all season as a mercurial forward in the Toby Greene mould.

Van Hattum is the ideal selection if he gets through to pick 5, but Gus Teixeira has plenty of fans and remains in this section of the crop as a damaging forward-half midfielder with power and scoreboard impact.

The Tigers will add a second round pick to their arsenal through a compensation pick on night two and it's a good spot to add run and dare on the outside. Jackson Phillips has a high floor as a wingman with clean hands and good foot skills, George Gale offers a bigger body and the running power to play peripheral positions and Jake Eime should be a real consideration if he slips through as a speedster out of the backline.

NGA prospect Tanner Armstrong may get through to the category B rookie list.

St Kilda
Draft picks: 10, 16, 41, 51, 69, 87, 105

List needs: Key position depth, inside ball-winner

The Saints have undergone a list transformation over the past few years and now own two quality picks after dealing Rowan Marshall to Geelong. They're in a great position to address areas of need and appear unlikely to trade up from these spots.

At pick 10 local product Tyson Bradley will be right in the frame. He has the body to play senior football at some point next year and is reliable in his defensive instincts and composed ball use. He would immediately compete for a spot alongside Cal Wilkie and Jack Silvagni. At the other end of the ground Sam Gayfer and Wil Malady are very different types of key forward prospects. Gayfer is brave and strong in the air with the biggest leap recorded in combine history. Malady can play up the ground with an elite work rate and is dangerous closer to home as an aerialist that butters up at ground level.

Lochie Burrows has been closely linked with the Dragons product providing the toughness, running power and versatility Ross Lyon covets. He can play at either end before eventually moving on-ball, but the Saints would be risking losing out on him if they leave it to pick 16. Leo Steed remains a live option as a pure midfielder that can unlock the runners around him with clean hands in stoppages. The wildcard at this spot is Jack Pickett whose excellent forward craft saw him enter the season at the top key forward prospect before rupturing his ACL.

On night two the Saints can address forward-half woes with talent including powerful SA small Gabe Patterson or exciting goalkicker Marlon Neocleous. Depending on their first two selections, the talls around the mark will include WA's Harvey Spawton-Guy and Knights defender Tate Hodgson.

Sydney
Draft picks: 6, 38, 39, 47, 54, 76, 95, 113

List needs: Key defensive talent, midfield youth

The Swans have their first top 10 pick since taking Logan McDonald and Braeden Campbell in 2020, courtesy of Nick Blakey's exit.

It's a good spot to swoop on any slider out of the top bracket of the open pool. A quality key defensive prospect will be circled on the whiteboard with SA's Mitch Harris the standout this year. He's the all-round package that can lockdown and intercept with safe hands and good closing speed. If there was a name to slide it could be Gus Teixeira, a powerful forward-half midfielder that will eventually become a full-time on-baller.

Expect Sydney to have a good look at a bid on Ethan Matthews out of the Giants Academy, which GWS will promptly match. They may be on the receiving end of an early bid themselves, with Mason McGroder attracting plenty of attention as early as the second round. The champion long jumper has chosen to pursue football and, while raw, he offers incredible upside as a defender that attacks the ball in the air.

As a key forward that can impact right away, Jack Slattery was the best-performed player at the national championships and is just one year older than the draft class. The SA prospect is slightly undersized at 192cm but is a beautiful set shot and creates separation on the lead. His range begins in the 30s. Koby LeCras has a chance to be on the board still after a partial tear of his ACL, but the hard-running forward can play a variety of roles at 192cm including up on a wing or deep forward.

West Coast
Draft picks: 3, 23, 58, 64, 73, 82, 100 (plus second round compensation pick)

List needs: Best available talent

West Coast have another top pick to capitalise on as their list build takes shape. They're right in the frame to snap up the most highly-touted WA prospect since Luke Jackson, with classy midfielder Heath Mellody deserving of a top five pick this year. Beginning his season out of defence, Mellody blossomed on-ball winning the Larke Medal and dominating in patches at WAFL level for Claremont. He has an insatiable work ethic and uses the ball well in space, attributes that pair well alongside Harley Reid and Willem Duursma in the engine room.

It's not a foregone conclusion that the Eagles opt for the local product. Expect them to heavily consider Arki Butler if the goalkicker is on the board still with a real need to add firepower to the forward 50 alongside Jake Waterman. Ethan Drever's power out of the contest will also be coveted and it would be another Vic Country prospect to join the pick one duo.

There's a familial connection with the nephew of 2018 premiership forward Mark LeCras. Koby possesses real talent at 192cm with his running, smarts and goal sense allowing him to play inside 50 or up on a wing. He's a second round option, as is hard nut Noah Williams whose courage in the clinches and capacity to play with defensive intent has value. Local product George Gale has the frame to play early through the midfield and wings in this range as well.

The Eagles will look to trade one of their second round selections for a 2026 first-rounder with an eye towards capital for a Chad Warner play. Add to it that James Artemis is a top prospect in the crop out of Western Australia.

It comes with the list crunch - West Coast has three spots to use at the national draft and will be keen to secure father-son Harper Banfield after missing on brother Charlie last year. Halfback Garrison Kenh and father-son Noah Braun will be rookie considerations.

Western Bulldogs
Draft picks: 42, 53, 55, 83, 89, 91, 109

List needs: Reliable role players, small forward depth

The Dogs did their work at the trade period by securing Zak Butters via free agency and a multi-club trade. It means they enter proceedings late on night two with an eye towards talented NGA forward Khaled El Souki. He's rated around the top 20 but may slide due to the depth of the crop which will make for an easier time matching a bid for the Dogs.

They addressed their key defensive dearth with Jordon Butts but should still have a look at Xavier Ladbrook as a long-term piece, and there are more defensive options in Darcy Szerszyn and Billy Wigmore that could be available later in the draft. Wigmore is a local Western Jets product alongside Lachie Hicks whose athletic traits through the midfield are tempting.

stories.headline: WNBA Finals saw surge in attendance, record ratings
stories.summary: The WNBA Finals were the most watched since 1999, with an average of 1.88 million people viewing the seven-game series that Golden State won over Atlanta in a decisive
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- The WNBA Finals were the most watched since 1999, with an average of 1.88 million people viewing the series that Golden State won over Atlanta in a decisive Game 7.

That game averaged 3.3 million viewers, making it the most-watched WNBA postseason game ever. It was up 128% from last season's clinching game between Las Vegas and Phoenix that the Aces won.

All seven games in the series were sold out, including Game 6, which was played at 12:30 p.m. ET.

The Finals capped the WNBA's most-watched postseason since its inaugural season in 1997, averaging 1.49 million viewers, up 27% from last year.

stories.headline: Kangaroos raring for rowdy Samoan semifinal
stories.summary: Picked ahead of James Tedesco for Sunday's semi-final against Samoa, Kangaroos fullback Reece Walsh says team success outweighs any battle for the No.1 jersey.
stories.body:
Reece Walsh is locked in as fullback for Australia's World Cup semi-final, but refuses to accept he has truly beaten out two-time Dally M Medal winner James Tedesco for the Kangaroos' No.1 jersey.

After coach Kevin Walters split the games between the two superstars in group play, Walsh has been given the nod to start Sunday's semi-final against Samoa.

However, the 24-year-old rejects the notion that he's nailed down the position, with Tedesco still waiting in the wings fresh off an NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

"I wouldn't say anyone's cemented on a spot," Walsh said.

"There's (six) on the bench now, so I could get hooked and replaced."

Tedesco sported the No.1 jersey when the Kangaroos won the 2022 World Cup, beating Samoa 30-10 in the final, and the veteran is offering plenty of advice to the new first-choice fullback.

"Building the game early through the middle, and a lot of that push-support stuff," Walsh told media when asked about Tedesco's biggest tips for him.

"We're two completely different players, but to be able to pick his brain about his strengths and what he brings to the team, I'm really grateful to have these opportunities to be around quality players like him."

That camaraderie characterises the Kangaroos' camp, with players willing to sacrifice their own playing minutes for the good of the team.

"I wouldn't say it's too much competing against each other, I feel like it's trying to get the best out of the whole team," the Brisbane Broncos superstar said.

"You worry about your own job, and focus on doing your role really well for the team."

Latrell Mitchell is one player taking on a new role, the South Sydney star lining up on the bench for the must-win semi-final.

The centre admits he may be the "worst spectator ever'' waiting impatiently on the sideline, but says there are no bruised egos for any of the Kangaroos not starting.

"I don't think you have an ego in any team," Mitchell said.

"We all play a part and a role, and we all have a set goal. We're a collective really chasing something, and that's the World Cup.''

The 29-year-old, who has played 10 Tests for Australia, is happy to offer any advice he can to Kotoni Staggs and Bradman Best, who will start in the centres.

"I love Kotoni, I love Bradman Best, and I just love seeing them play," Mitchell said.

"They're unbelievable athletes, and if I can add value or have a presence with them, I take a lot of pride in that, my role is to be a good teammate."
